bib.title: Bias and Fairness in Large Language Models: A Survey

read.skipped: References (from ~204000 chars) skimmed for lineage only.

question: How can social bias and fairness in LLMs be defined, measured (metrics, datasets) and mitigated, and what are the limits of each approach?
contributions: Consolidation and formalization of social bias and fairness definitions for NLP, with a taxonomy of harms and fairness desiderata
Survey and taxonomy of metrics for bias evaluation (embedding, probability, generated text)
Survey and taxonomy of datasets for bias evaluation (counterfactual inputs, prompts), with public compilation
Survey and taxonomy of mitigation techniques by intervention stage (pre-, in-, intra-, post-processing)

results.claim: The survey organises bias-evaluation metrics into three classes by what they use from the model: embeddings, probabilities, generated text.
results.setup: Survey of metrics for LLM bias evaluation (Sec 3, Table 3)
results.quote: Most bias evaluation metrics for LLMs can be categorized by what they use from the model such as the embeddings, probabilities, or generated text.

results.claim: Mitigation techniques are organised by intervention stage into four stages (pre-, in-, intra-, post-processing) with 13 named mechanisms in Table 5.
results.setup: Table 5 and Sec 5 of the survey
results.quote: pre-processing (modifying model inputs), in-training (modifying the optimization process), intra-processing (modifying inference behavior), and post-processing (modifying model outputs)
results.note: Table 5 lists 5 pre-processing, 4 in-training, 3 intra-processing, 1 post-processing mechanisms (13 total, counted by the reader, not stated by the authors).

results.claim: Social bias is split into 7 representational harms and 2 allocational harms.
results.quote: representational harms (misrepresentation, stereotyping, disparate system performance, derogatory language, and exclusionary norms) and allocational harms (direct discrimination and indirect discrimination)
results.note: Prose lists 5 representational harms, Table 1 lists 7 (adds Erasure and Toxicity); 7+2=9 follows Table 1.

results.claim: Embedding-based bias has weak or no reliable relationship to downstream-task bias (Goldfarb-Tarrant et al. 2021 find no reliable correlation).
results.source: Goldfarb-Tarrant et al. 2021; Cabello et al. 2023; Orgad and Belinkov 2022
results.setup: Embedding-based metrics (WEAT, SEAT, CEAT) vs downstream tasks
results.quote: Goldfarb-Tarrant et al. (2021) find no reliable correlation at all

results.claim: Decoding parameters (tokens generated, temperature, top-k) can flip conclusions of generated-text bias metrics on the same dataset.
results.setup: Generated text-based metrics on open-ended generation datasets
results.quote: can drastically change the level of bias, which can lead to contradicting results for the same metric with the same evaluation datasets

results.claim: Expected Maximum Toxicity is computed over 25 generations per prompt (RealToxicityPrompts protocol).
results.setup: Perspective API toxicity score, mean and std reported
results.quote: Gehman et al. (2020) leverage Expected Maximum Toxicity (EMT) computed over 25 generations

results.claim: Toxicity Probability counts a prompt as toxic if at least one of its generations scores 0.5 or higher.
results.quote: generating at least one text with a toxicity score ≥0.5 over the 25 generations

results.claim: Blodgett et al. 2021 find ambiguity about what stereotype is captured in nearly half of instances of Winogender, WinoBias, StereoSet and CrowS-Pairs.
results.quote: In nearly half of all instances, these datasets contain ambiguities about what stereotypes they capture

results.claim: Meaning-preserving edits (synonyms, adjectives) to Winogender and Bias NLI can drastically change bias scores.
results.quote: small changes to Winogender and Bias NLI’s datasets that do not meaningfully change semantics

results.quote: Crowdsourced Stereotype Pairs (CrowS-Pairs) (Nangia et al. 2020) provides 1,508

results.quote: StereoSet presents 16,995 crowdsourced instances

results.quote: is a question-answering dataset of 58,492 examples

results.quote: providing 100,000 sentence prefixes curated from web text

results.claim: Pruning 10-20% of parameters with WANDA increases resistance to jailbreaking; heavier pruning is harmful.
results.setup: Safety alignment robustness, hate speech and discriminatory generations
results.quote: pruning 10-20% of model parameters increases resistance to jailbreaking

results.claim: Pruning 30% or more of parameters raised gender, race and religion bias in hate-speech classifiers.
results.quote: models with pruning of 30% or more of the original parameters demonstrate increased levels of gender, race, and religious bias

results.claim: Gira et al. 2022 freeze over 99% of parameters, tuning layer norm or position embeddings, on WinoBias and CrowS-Pairs.
results.quote: Gira, Zhang, and Lee (2022) freeze over 99% of a model’s parameters

results.claim: Thakur et al. 2023 debias with as few as 10 curated examples.
results.setup: Gender bias fine-tuning set built by masking and predicting gender words
results.quote: as few as 10 examples of the most biased examples

results.claim: Borchers et al. 2022 build a low-bias job-ad set from the 10% least biased examples.
results.setup: Job advertisements, gendered word list frequency
results.quote: selecting the 10% least biased

results.claim: Prompt instructions asking for diversity or gender equality did not remove bias (Borchers et al. 2022); biased and unbiased prompts gave similar outputs (Li and Zhang 2023).
results.source: Borchers et al. 2022; Li and Zhang 2023
results.quote: find instructions that prompt diversity or gender equality to be unsuccessful

results.claim: Toxicity-reducing decoding can amplify bias by suppressing minority dialects such as African-American English (Xu et al. 2021).
results.setup: Decoding strategy modification with toxic-token heuristics
results.quote: techniques that reduce toxicity can in turn amplify bias by not generating minority dialects

results.claim: Wang et al. 2022 politeness rewrite corpus: 10K human rewrites and 100K model rewrites.
results.quote: The dataset contains 10K human-based rewrites, and 100K model-based rewrites

limits: Authors concede a technical-solutionist framing: taxonomies are organised by implementation, not by downstream harm or context (Sec 7).
Covers only model training and evaluation, not problem formulation, data collection or deployment (Sec 7).
Authors note empirical comparisons of in-training mitigations are very limited and few studies compare techniques across stages (Sec 5.2.5, 6.4).
Survey reports no experiments of its own; every quantitative result is quoted from other work.
Predates 2024-era instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned chat models as targets; most surveyed metrics assume BERT-era masked models or GPT-2 style completion.
practices: Do not use embedding- or probability-based metrics as the sole bias metric; pair them with a direct downstream-task evaluation (Sec 3.6 rec 1).
Report model specification, decoding parameters, prompts and templates with every bias metric (Sec 3.6 rec 2; Sec 3.5.4).
Construct metrics that reflect real-world power dynamics and state the targeted harm explicitly (Sec 3.6 rec 3).
Check datasets for construct, content and ecological validity before use; be cautious with counterfactual perturbation datasets (Sec 4.3 rec 1).
Use datasets covering more than gender and stereotyping, and treat US-centric datasets as weak proxies elsewhere (Sec 4.3 rec 2).
Avoid mitigation that merely masks or swaps identity words, which flattens power imbalances (Sec 5.5 rec 1).
State the fairness assumption encoded in a loss or reward; consider cost-sensitive learning for minority classes (Sec 5.5 rec 2).
Validate that toxicity heuristics in decoding do not filter out minority dialects (Sec 5.5 rec 3).
Do not erase social group identity when rewriting outputs (Sec 5.5 rec 4).
Make bias and fairness evaluation a standard part of model documentation; consider audits and adversarial testing beyond static benchmarks (Sec 6.3).

terms.definition: disparate treatment or outcomes between social groups that arise from historical and structural power asymmetries
(approximate) parity across all groups, up to epsilon, of a statistical outcome measure conditioned on group membership
individuals similar with respect to some task should be treated similarly
Denigrating and subordinating attitudes towards a social group (derogatory language, disparate system performance, erasure, exclusionary norms, misrepresentation, stereotyping, toxicity)
Disparate distribution of resources or opportunities between social groups (direct and indirect discrimination)
a social group is not explicitly used, such that M(X) = M(X without A)
M(Xi) and M(Xj) are identical under some invariance metric
a neutral word is equally likely regardless of social group
protected attribute words for different social groups are equally likely in a neutral context
conditional probability of a neutral word in generated output equals its conditional probability in a reference dataset
Local bias is a property of word-context associations; global bias is a property of an entire span of text
modify the model's behavior without further training or fine-tuning to generate debiased predictions at inference
replacing protected attribute words, such as gendered pronouns, to achieve a balanced dataset
